meta.titre: Elections and Voting: how citizens choose and decide
meta.sous_theme: Elections, referendums, voting conditions and electoral fraud

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L Citizenship Education past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: Before every election, radio stations in Bafoussam, Bamenda and Douala remind residents to check that their names are on the electoral list. A citizen who forgets to register, or who stays at home on polling day, loses a chance to help choose who will run the council or the country. Elections and referendums are favourite topics at the GCE because they link the Constitution, the rights of citizens and the daily life of the nation. Paper 1 tests the meaning of key terms and the effects of electoral fraud, while Paper 2 asks you to list conditions and explain points in full sentences.

items: A citizen is a person who belongs to a country and has rights and duties in it.
In a democracy, the people are the source of the authority of the government.
A political party is a group of people who share ideas and try to win power by peaceful means.

sections.contenu_markdown:
### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Election | A process in which citizens choose leaders or representatives by voting |
| Suffrage | The right to vote. Universal adult suffrage means that every adult citizen who meets the legal conditions may vote |
| Electoral register | The official list of citizens who may vote in a given area |
| Voter's card | The document that proves a person is registered and may vote |
| Constituency | The area whose voters choose a representative |
| Turnout | The share of registered voters who actually vote |
| Referendum | A direct vote in which the whole nation answers YES or NO to one question |

### Conditions and organisation
The electoral law decides who may vote and who may stand as a candidate. Typical conditions are being a citizen, having reached the age fixed by law, being registered on the electoral register and not being disqualified by law or by a court. A candidate for a municipal council is normally presented by a political party on a list and must also meet the conditions set by the law. In Cameroon, Elections Cameroon (ELECAM) is the body in charge of organising and supervising elections and referendums.

### Kinds of vote
Cameroonians take part in presidential, legislative, municipal, regional and senatorial elections. A referendum is different: citizens do not choose a person, they decide a single issue, for example a proposed change to an important law.

### A free and fair election
- The electoral register is accurate and open to checking.
- The ballot is secret, so nobody can punish a voter for a choice.
- Every vote has the same value.
- All candidates follow the same rules during the campaign.
- Counting is done in public and the results are announced honestly.
- Complaints are settled by the courts or the body named by law.

### Election rigging
Rigging means any dishonest act meant to change the result: buying votes, stuffing ballot boxes, voting more than once, voting in another person's name, frightening voters or falsifying figures. Its effects include loss of public trust, low turnout in later elections, violence, a government that many people refuse to accept, and a bad image abroad.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks for preconditions, requirements or qualities
variantes.contenu_markdown: Begin with the sentence 'The electoral law requires that...'. Give separate points: citizenship, the minimum age fixed by law, registration on the electoral register, a clean legal record, and for a candidate the backing of a party list where the law asks for it. Add a short reason for each point to earn the full marks of a 6-mark question.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When two ideas must be distinguished
variantes.contenu_markdown: An election chooses people for office and offers several candidates. A referendum asks the voters to approve or reject one proposal with a YES or NO. In both cases the people take part directly, but the question put to them is different.

Name the effect, then explain it in one more sentence. For example: 'Loss of confidence in the system. Citizens who believe that results are decided in advance stop voting and stop respecting the leaders.' Group your points into political, social and economic effects.

sections.enonce_markdown: Write the model answer to this question: (a) Define the term 'electoral register'. (b) Explain three ways in which ordinary citizens can help to make an election free and fair. [8 marks]

etapes.justification: 'Define' wants a short exact meaning. 'Explain' wants each point developed. Three ways means three separate points.
A definition names the thing, says what it is and what it is for.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The electoral register is the official list of all citizens who are entitled to vote in an area.

etapes.justification: Pick actions that citizens themselves can perform, and that cover different stages: before, during and after voting.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Registering and checking the list; voting peacefully and keeping the ballot secret; reporting or refusing fraud and accepting honest results.

etapes.action: Develop each way with a reason.
etapes.justification: A mark is given for the point and another for the explanation.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Registering gives a true list; refusing a bribe stops vote buying; accepting honest results keeps peace.

etapes.justification: It shows that you have answered the question as a whole.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Citizens help an election because the quality of the vote depends on the behaviour of voters.

sections.conclusion_markdown:
(a) The electoral register is the official list of all citizens who are entitled to vote in a given area.

(b) First, citizens can register and check their names on the register, so that the list is accurate and nobody votes twice or in another person's name. Second, they can refuse bribes and threats and cast their vote freely and secretly, which stops vote buying and intimidation. Third, they can accept results that are honest, report cases of fraud to the proper authorities and avoid violence, so that disputes are settled peacefully by the law. In all, the quality of an election depends greatly on the behaviour of the voters themselves.

items.erreur_markdown: A student writes: 'A referendum is the election of the President.'
items.pourquoi_faux: A referendum is not the choice of a person. Voters answer YES or NO to a question.
items.correction_markdown: A referendum is a direct vote of citizens on a single issue, answered YES or NO.

items.erreur_markdown: A student answers a question on 'preconditions' by writing only: 'voting, campaigning, winning'.
items.pourquoi_faux: These are stages of an election, not conditions that a person must fulfil.
items.correction_markdown: Give conditions such as citizenship, minimum legal age, registration on the electoral register and not being disqualified.

items.erreur_markdown: A student states that 'a secret ballot means that nobody knows who won'.
items.pourquoi_faux: Secrecy protects the voter's choice, not the result. The result is made public.
items.correction_markdown: A secret ballot means that nobody can find out how a particular person voted.

items.erreur_markdown: A student names only one consequence of rigging and repeats it in three sentences.
items.pourquoi_faux: The examiner awards marks for different points, not for repetition.
items.correction_markdown: Give several different consequences (loss of trust, violence, low turnout, weak government) and explain each briefly.

items.erreur_markdown: A student writes: 'Turnout is the number of candidates in an election.'
items.correction_markdown: Turnout is the share of registered voters who actually vote.

items.enonce_markdown: In an invented town, 8,000 citizens are registered to vote and 5,200 of them go to the polling stations. (a) Calculate the turnout as a percentage. (b) State two reasons why some registered voters may not vote.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Turnout = (voters who voted divided by registered voters) times 100 = 5,200 / 8,000 x 100 = **65%**.

(b) Award a mark for each valid reason, for example: illness or travel on polling day; lack of trust that the vote will count; difficulty in reaching the polling station; lack of interest or information.

items.enonce_markdown: Distinguish between an election and a referendum, and give one example of a decision that could be put to a referendum.
items.solution_markdown: Award marks for the following. An election is a vote in which citizens choose persons (or parties) to hold office, such as councillors or members of the National Assembly. A referendum is a vote in which citizens answer YES or NO to one question, so they decide an issue and not a person. An example of a question suited to a referendum is a proposal to change an important law of the nation, such as the Constitution. **Election = choosing persons; referendum = deciding one issue.**

items.enonce_markdown: In the same invented town, a candidate obtains 2,080 of the 5,200 votes cast. (a) Calculate the percentage of the votes cast that he obtains. (b) Suppose that the polling officers add 700 false ballots in his favour. Explain three effects of such rigging on the town.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) 2,080 / 5,200 x 100 = **40%**.

(b) Award marks for three explained effects. First, loss of trust: voters who learn of the fraud no longer believe in the system. Second, tension or violence: supporters of other candidates may protest, and clashes can destroy property and lives. Third, a weak local government: leaders whose position is disputed find it hard to collect taxes and lead development projects. Other valid effects: low turnout in the next election, a poor image of the town, and delays in public work.

items_markdown: An election lets citizens choose representatives, and a referendum lets them decide one issue by answering YES or NO.
To vote, a person must meet the conditions of the electoral law, notably citizenship, legal age and registration.
A free and fair election has an accurate register, a secret ballot, equal rules for all candidates, open counting and a lawful way to settle complaints.
Rigging is any dishonest act that changes the result, and its effects include loss of trust, violence, low turnout and a poor image abroad.
Turnout = voters who voted divided by registered voters, times 100.
In 'preconditions' and 'consequences' questions, give separate points and explain each one.
